The Government General in making this publicly known for the information and compliance ot all concerned with the admonition that these Conventions of His Majesty will most rigidly be enforced, thinks it proper especially to recommend attention to the Otli Article of the additional Clause of the Convention ol the 22nd March 1833, which is of the following tenor ; þÿ Any merchant vessel of either of the two Nations visited and detained in pursuance of the Convention of the 30th of November 1831, and ot the provisions hereinbefore recited, shall, unless proof he given to the contrary, he held and taken ot right to have engaged in tip Slave trade, or to have been fitted out for the purposes of such traftick, if any of the particulars hereinafter specified shall be found in her outiit or equipment, or on board ol her videlicet : ll> Having her hatches fitted with open gratings, instead ot being close hatches, as usual in merchant-vessels; 2 Having more divisions or bulkheads in the hold, < >r on deck, than necessary lor trading vessels ; 3' Having on board spare planks, either actually fitted in that shape, or tit lor readily laying a second or moveable deck, or slave deck : 4 Having on board shackles, holts, or hand cull's : 5 Having on board a supply of water, more than sufficient lor the consumption of

her crew, as a merchant vessel ; ti Having on board an unreasonable number of water casks, or oilier vessels for holding water, unless the master shall produce a certilicate from the Custom-House from the place at which he cleared outwards, stating that a sulHcicnt security had been given bv the owners ol such vessel, that such casks, or other vessels, should only be used for the reception ol palm oil, or he employed in any other lawful trade ; 7 Having on board a greater quantity of mess tubs, or kids, than requisite for the use of her crew, as merchant- vessel ; N Having on hoard two or more copper boileis, or even one evidently larger than requisite for the use of her crew, as a merchant vessel ; 9 Having on hoard a quantity of rice or farinba, Hour ot the manioc of Brazil, or cassada, or maize, or Indian corn, beyond probable requisite provision for the use of her crew, and such rice, flour, maize, or Indian corn, not being entered on the manifest as part of the cargo for trade. Extraordinaiy Effect of Music. A Paris þÿ Paper contains the following extraordinary story: þÿ A woman, twenty-eight years age, of residing at a village in Piedmont, where she was born, bad never heard any music until a short time since, when she was taken to a ball, at which there w as a very excellent orchestra. During the whole of the performances she rein, -lined in a sort of stupor, and when the concert was over she appeared to be suffering under great emotion. From that time, walking or sleeping, the melodious sounds were continually heard by her, and eventually she could not sleep at all. A state of apathy ensued, which led to a total derangement of the vital function. Several physicians were called in, who prescribed all sorts of remedies, but without success. Weakness and consumption ensued. The pulse became irregular, and the general effect was the same as that caused by sudden fright. She became at length extremely nervous and weak, arid died in about a month from the time when she first heard the music. She never ceased however to hear the airs, and tliev seemingly became louder and more powerful as she gradually

X u W T Hi THE MERVHAA FS CLERK. Upon my life 1 cannot think Why I was put in trade ; For such a calling, 1 am sure, 1 never could be made. For money 1 don't care a jot, In specs I'd ne'er embark þÿ | I would not wish the devil worse Than be a merchant's clerk.

Ere wide awake and breakfast o'er, To business I must run; Thro' town 1 go. in sun or rain, A sort of living dun Without success, the ruler's frown, While debtors call you shark, þÿ Thus smiles and sunshine seldom beam To greet a merchant's clerk. Oft. poring o'er the books, I've wished The ledger decay, in The waste book wasted, and have d þÿ d The journal every day. To invoice, bill, and policy I've long'd to set a spark, For all the troubles they have heaped Upon a merchant's cicrk.

I've written one þÿ two vols, romance, And tales I'm sure by scores, þÿ My poetry, I have been told, Is quite as good as Moore's; But what's the use of writing rhymes' That no one will remark, þÿ The VI use herself would not be read W as she a merchant's clerk.

I'm not awkward in the dance, I'm told I'm not by any means An ugly looking man ; But mothers all are wrapt in frowns, And cast their giances dark, On daughters who too kindly smile Upon a merchant's clerk.
Tlicy tell me, in some forty years, They'll take me in the firm,
For some long greedy worm. What's riches when we can't enjoy No frolics, fun, nor larks, þÿ Oh ! little boys and unborn babes, Now don't be merchant's clerks.

crjri oitsu Approach of Haixky's Comet. þÿ Professor Littrovv, the astronomer, of Vienna, has just published a pamphlet on Halley's comet, entitled " Beytrage zu einer Monographic des Hallevshen Cometen," (Materials for a Monography ot Halicy s Comet) which is illustrated by two maps. The calculations ol Prolessor' L.ittrow are founded on the elements given by M. De Pontecouiant, and determine the 7th of November as the day on which the comet will reach its perihelion ; at this point it w ill be 12,069,000 German miles, 55,- or 56 1,400 English miles, distant from the sun. tin the 8th ol Octobi r of the same year the comet will approach nearest to the earth, when it will be only 3," 19,000 German miles, or 1 .107,460 English miles, distant from it. It will be first visible in the month of April next, as a morning star in Taurus : but its light w ill lie very feeble, as the ravs will have to traverse 185 millions of miles in reaching us. Its motion will then be in the plane ol the earth's orbit, and, therefore, its progress will be hardly perceptible. From Taurus it will pass into the constellation Gemini, and its rising will precede the dawn by an interval progressively increasing. It will be best seen during the month ot October, and it its constitution has not been modified since its last revolution, it will be accompanied by a tail of considerable length. The comet, after passing its perihelion, will again approach the earth at the commencement of the year 1836. In the month of March of that year, it will

be at a distance of upwards of 1 16 millions of miles from the earth, and will re-appear in the constellations Corvus and Crater; alter which þÿ it will disappear, and will not be seen again until February, 1912.

One of the most cautious systems of education ever known, was that pursued with the voting Count I) , of Berlin. Among otner rigorous restrictions, he was never allowed to walk out except in fine weather, and then only in the company of his tutor; this bad the effect of creating in his mind the singular desire to be thoroughly drenched with rain, but his wishes remained unaccomplished, for he was mighty vigilantly watched : at length it so happened that during a heavy fall ol ruin,

the tutor was suddenly called away ; he took care, however, first to secure the door, and had scarcely left the room, when the youthful Count threw open the window, mounted a chair, and leaned out as far as possible. He was charmed with the cold bath, but hearing the returning footsteps of the tutor, he attempted to spring front the chair, when his foot slipped, he fell from the window, and broke his neck.

Hiring a Coachman. þÿ I had a master once who had two beautiful English horses, and he wanted a careful man to drive them ; he was a mighty pleasant gentleman þÿ the sort of master who would knock a man down for the least thing in the world þÿ and so good-hearted when the passion was over. Well, there was as many as fifteen after the place, and the first that wint up to him, " Well, my man," says he, how near the edge of a precipice " would you undertake to drive my carriage So the boy considered, and he says, says lie. " Within a foot, plaze yer honour, and no harm" " Very well," says he, "go down, and I'll give ye vcr answer by and by." So the next came up, and said he'd be bound to carry 'em within half a foot; and the next said six inches ; and another, a dandyfied chap n.in< iy, was so mighty nice, that he would drive it within "three inches and a half, he'd go bail." Well, at last my turn came, and when l is honour asked me how nigh 1 would drive I is carriage to a precipice, 1 said, says 1, " I'iaze yer honour, I'd keep as far off it as I could." " Very well, Misther Byrne," says he " you're my coachman," says he. Oeh, the roar there was in the kitchen, whin 1 wint down and tould the joke! Well, I was there better nor two years, and at the end 1 lost it through a little mistake. I was drowsy one night coming home, and faith the horses had a spite tome, on account of my counthrv. and they took a wrong turn, and stuck last in a gap ' and sure it's rewarded 1 ought to have been

instead of punished, for sorra a one but myself would ever have got the horses and carriage out of the gap without a scratch or a brack upon them ; but there's no justice in this world." þÿ New Monthly Magazine.

In this sense it may be singly used to denote a person sent from God; and consequently by way of antonomasis, or expressing the dignity of the person, instead of the name, it became peculiarly appropriate to the birth day, or incarnation, of that most Holy and divine Spirit, who came from Goo, as the Minister of Ins will, and the Messenger of his grace, to man. The name of Messiah has been applied to the Kings of Judah, and even to the Prophets and High Priests of the Jews; and was designed significant, as not only ot their mental qualifications, but of those gifts and graces of the spirit of the almighty, so essentially requisite for properly discharging the duties of those important offices : but the title ot Messiah was principally, and by way of preeminence, given by the Hebrews to their expected great Deliverer; whom our Saviour expressly declared himself to have been ; and thenceforward Christ, the equivalent ot Messiah, was made an addition to Jesus, the name designed him from Heaven, by the angel Gahrii l, and which signified Saviour, or the important mission our Lord had undertaken for the rescuing mankind irom the dire eflccts

of sin, by bis atoning sacrifice. Whatever difference of opinion may arise with regard to the actual time of our Saviour's birth, surely all persons may join in the offices which have, with so much judgment, been expressly appointed for the solemnization of that joyous event ; as the season which the church has chosen, docs not involve the credibility of the fact, nor affect any material point, either practical or devotional. From CrabbeU Poithumout Poemi . ) There is within the world in which we dwell A friendship, answering to that world full well; An interchange of looks and actioni kind, And, in souie sense, an intercourse of imud ; A useful commerce, a conrenient trade, By which both parties are the happier made : And, when the thing is rightly understood And justly valued, it is wise and good.

I speak not here of friendships that excite In hoys Bt school such Wonder and delight, Of high heroic friends, in serious strife, Contending which should yield a forfeit life þÿ Such woudrous love, in their maturer days, Men, if they credit, are conteut to praise.

I speak not here of friendships true and just, When friend can friend with life aud honour trust; Where mind to mind has long familiar grown, Aud every failing, every virtue known. Of these I speak not; things so rich and rare, That we degrade with jewels to compare, Or bullion pure and massy. I intend, To treat of one whose neighbour called him friend, Or called him neighbour ; and with reason good- The friendship rising from the neighbourhood. A sober kind, in common service known; Not such as is iu death and peril shown ; Such as will give or ask a helping hand, But no important sacrifice demand ; In fact, a friendship that will long abide, If seldom reshly, never strongly tried. Yes ! these are sober friendships, made for use ; And much convenience they in life produce. Like a good coat, that keeps us from the cold, The cloth of frieze is not a clolh of gold ; But neither is il piebald, pieced, and poor ; Tis a good useful coat, and nothing more.

This day the Court of Chancery was excessively crowded in consequence of the Lord Chancellor's expected farewell address. þÿ Among the few motions made was one hy Mr. Pitt, who observed, in the course of his statement, that he hoped his Lordship would see justice done to him before he left the Court, his Lordship's absence from which he irusted was to be of short duration; it being as he (Mr. Pitt) understood for some temporary purpose. The Lord Chancellor : I hope not ; i hope it will be for ever. At 2 o'clock the Lord Chancellor addressed the Bar þÿ "1 have now disposed of all the cases that have been heard before me up to the last; and it is with great satisfaction that I quit this Court without putting any one party to the expcnce and delay of having his case To-heard before another Judge. There are only two cases which remain to be heard, which were set down before the last long vacation. As I have no right to press the parties closer than this, it was my intention, if I had remained here, to adjourn the Court on the last day of term, early next week, until the 11th of January, the first day of next term, as I was obliged to do in the month of June last, for a like reason, the business being all disposed of. Thus, 1 have the great saiisfaction of reflecting that this ,'ourt, represented by its enemies as the temple of discord, delay, and expence, has been twice closed

within the space of five months ; and I ascribe this singular felicity of the times, to the tried ability and indefatigable industry of my most fcarncd and excellent coadjutors, the present Vicc-Chanccllor, and my most learned and

®Asrs3t TasjfastaasK aa-oaaaaira ATKS. ever-to-be-Iamentcd friend, the late Master of the Rolls ; and in part, also, to the labour and talent, and indefatigable research of this most able and independent Bar. That the same good fortune will lollow my successor. 1 confidently expect ; for he, too, will have the aid of his Honour, the Vice-Chancellor, and he will have the further aid of the present Master of the Rolls, whose high accomplishments as a lawyer, whose consummate fitness for the judicial oifice, render his elevation at once the greatest benefit to the public, and my own best title to the gratitude of the prolession." When his Lordship came to that passage which alludes to the late Master of the Rolls, his voice failed him, and he was for perhaps a minute unable to proceed. When he did so, it was with broken voice and uncontrollable emotion. At the conclusion of his brief address, his Lordship rose, bowed hastily, but profoundly, to the Bar, and instantly quitted the Court. Lord Brougham then proceeded to St. James's, and delivered up the Great Seal. who would br an editor? Reader ! you know very little about the life of an editor, ond it is not worth while fn us to try to tell you u hat sort of a life he. leads. Payer, ink and types can't describe it. Pencil and /laint may be essayed in vain. To know how an editor lives, you must þÿ become an editor. But we say to you, as we have said to a'mnst every one who has ever thought it worth while to advise with us on the subject, þÿ don't try it, we beseech you. Stick to the lap stone þÿ the shears þÿ the. sledge þÿ the ho nilsaw the plough the pestle þÿ þÿ þÿ or even be a lawyer, ami whistle for clients þÿ and you may chance to 1 go ahead' þÿ but as you value i/niet and consistency, as you wish to have comfort by day, and rest by night, don't he an editor! l)o you ask why Jus' think for a m anent, what an ei/itor must do, and what h" wist not do, and your question will be answered. lie must have his paper well spiced with, political matter, but not too spicy. lie must go before his party and give tone to its proceedings, but he must not think of leading a party. He must publish all the news; and he must net publish any thing that is not founded in fact. He must endeavor to raise the standard of public morals, but lie must not attack any vice, or error, or infirmity, to which any of his patrons, or friend sore subject. He must write, whether he is gloomy or gladsome ; sick or well ; whether the mercury runs high or low ; whether political prospects are fait or foul : still, he must write; and he must produce something

that is either pretty or popular, or he is deemed a stupid fellow. lie must print whatever is sent or handed to him for insertion, whether he, can read it >r not ; let his space be little or much ; at the time, ami in the very manner that is requested. lie must remember and duly execute all orders verbal oi written, that his kind patrons arc so obliging as to dictate. lie must be, literally, ' all things to all men,' ' take the please every ' ol body and try to responsibility acting upon princi- ; or þÿ he must ple ; pursue an i tide pendant course ; labor to uphold the rights and liberties, and to improve the manners ami morals of his country : determine to be honest in the worst of times þÿ write like a freeman and toil like a slave ; wear out his types, finally himself, ami leave his children, (if he can keep the one and accumulate the other,) a good name, and a file of old newspapers!

THE VICTIM OF SEDUCTION. ( From an American paper.) Amelia F was one of those beings that nature decks in all its loveliness, arrayed in charms not acquired by artifice, but such as heaven had deservedly bestowed. She never experienced the soft blandishments of maternal affection, having been deprived of her mother in early infancy, befoie the tongue could lisp a parent's name, or the heart appreciate the gem thus immaturely torn from her. At the date of my acquaintance she had arrived at an age when the heart is most susceptible of love when the traces of that tender pas- þÿ sion leave an impression upon the mind that time can seldom obliterate. The spirit of happiness beamed in her cheerful countenance, and her jet black eyes rolling beneath their dark eyebrows, sparkled with animation and life ; the tender carmine played on her cheek, like the soft tinge of heaven's eternal day. The father of Amelia was gentleman a of information þÿ of sullen and morose disposition, though of stern integrity ; one that beheld the errors of mankind with contempt, and condemned them with a degree of harshness allied to scorn ; though he was aware that it was the lot of humanity to err, yet he was a sceptic in the belief that it was charitable to forgive. But with all his feelings he was comparatively genlle to his child ; even his harshness was sacrificed on the altar of paternal affection ; he beheld his tender plant of loveliness flourish beneatli the shelter of its parent stem, and would look forward with a father's

love, in the fond anticipation that it wouid, at some distant day, be an ornament and a prop of his decli ui 11 j; years ; too smooth the rugged path of life, and lighten the weight of age> while journeying to the tomb. Amelia enjoyed not alone a parent's love. She had a brother a few years older than herself, who had launched on the ocean of life, having left his home for the distant shores of Asia, where by his father's influence he had obtained a lucrative situation. M nitlis had rolled 011 since his departure, and time that often administers relief to the wretched, had dried the tear of affection from the cheek of the beautiful Amelia. Amelia still continued to grow in loveliness. The fame of her beauty extended far md wide, and drew around innumerable suitors ; yet he who fixed the unalterable affections of Amelia, was one of those characters who obtain the disgrace of being regarded as a model of that class of villains who select the fairest flowers as victims to their vanity þÿ reputation that is often with them equivalent to any kind of merit þÿ a fashionable butterfly roving from flower to flower to sip the honeyed sweetness from the rose of beauty. He was a gay, thoughtless youth, handsome in appearance, elegant an I refined in manners ; his serpent tongue could beguile the heart of purity ilsclf and plant the dagger of remorse within it þÿ The betrayal of innocence he considered an act worthy of commendation; such was Edgar Morton, that being to whom Amelia had en-

trusted her heart. She beheld in his treacherous smile, sincerity: not susceptible of vicious joy herself, she could only feel the raptures of a first affection. Moreton, to deceive the world and carry the appearance that his intentions were honorable, made overtures to Mr. F , who hesitated not a moment in rejecting them, llis

®Aira:R Tastrawaaas® m®®aamasr®a aths piercing eye and scrutinizing investigation had penetrated the veil that concealed the monsterþÿ he dismissed him and commanded Amelia, on the pain of his displeasure, to discountenance his addresses. This command, though from a beloved father, she dared to disobey, and in secret she cherished that passion that had become the food of her existence. # # #

It was on one of those delightful evenings when nature smiles in all its brilliancy þÿ when the high arch of heaven is lighted with its jewelled lamps þÿ that a coach was seen driving along the avenue that led to the seat of Mr. F , it stopped at an arbour, concealed from the mansion by the majestic oaks. It was there dorton was urging his victim on to crime, and offered his love as an apology for die inconsiderate step; he forced her credulity to believe, that on an elopement their future happiness depended, and that a few months would realize her utino-t desire þÿ a father's pardon and a husband's love His seductive language and winning smile conqucrred every scruple; intoxicated with love, she yielded to his intreaties, while the abyss of misery yawned beneath her. Mr. F , after the elopement of his daughter, settled into a despondency þÿ s"ldoff' his estate, and sailed for the West Indies, where, shortly after, he fell a victim to the scourge of the tropics, the yellow fever, leaving his property entirely to his son, who was at that time settled in Calcutta. Amelia was then residing in the city of New York, where she was only known as Morton's mistress. þÿ She had begun to experience that the path of illicit love led not to happiness, her ideal vision of felicity was a phantom of imagination that had flitted by like a summer cloud. In vain did she urge Edgar to iullil his promise of marriage ; to her entreaties he was deaf, and to her prayers he lent no ready ear; day after day he became

more inattentive, plunged more deeply into dissipation, and even in the presence of his profligate companions he insulted his victim. No attentions were paid to Amelia's supplications þÿ if she dared remonstrate she was repulsed with scorn þÿ he spurned the heart that adored him, and trampled 011 her whom he had ruined ; to complete her misery, he deserted tier. She now found herself abandoned, in a populous city, with no sympathising bosom to which she could fly to discharge the sorrows of her penitent heart, no ray to which she could turn tor consolation, for even the hope that lights the dull eye of grief had deserted her. Her own sex was the first to spurn her from their doors þÿ those who should have thrown the mantle of Charity over her to conceal her frailties, were the first to lacerate her wounded heart, no hand was extended to reclaim this erring child; the portals of mercy were shut ; she heard no consoling voice, bidding those without sin first cast a stone. Unfortunate woman ! One deviation from the track of virtue forever blasts thy name ; no tears of penitence can erase it from an uncharitable world. Men may out live their shame, and gain once more the eminence they lose; yet deprive a female of that valued gem, place but one single stain upon its escutcheon, and it never can he restored to its former lustre þÿ their star when set can rise no more, or if it should, its former brilliancy is forever obscure.

«% :jo, A year had fled since the deception of Mor ton, and Amelia, reduced to the last state ot wretchedness, was living on the charity ol the passing traveller. It was at this period that lli rnry had arrived, and having settled his business was preparing to return, as he was anxious to quit the country that reminded him only of the blasted hopes of a ruined sister. þÿ A li'w days prior to his departure, as 1 was returning with him from the dock to the hotel, we were accosted by a female dressed in the habiliments of poverty, whose sunken eve spoke the ravages of pollution. One single glance told Henry Iter wants, for he had an eye for pity, and a heart open as noon-day for heaven-born charity, llis purse was at once offered ; the liberality of the gift caused her to raise her eyes, when she discovered in the generous stranger her brother ! She uttered one piercing scream and would have fallen to the ground, had not my arm prevented her; the bonnet fell from her head, when the long beautiful hair that concealed her features was withdrawn, and though lingering years had chased the rose of beauty from her cheek s'lil tlie traces of its loveliness were left, and If ury beheld in the poor friendless beggar res'big 011 his bosom, his lost, degraded, and unfortunate sister. The novelty of the adventures had gathered a crowd around, one of whom was despatched for a coach, in which she was conveyed senseless to his lodgings. þÿ A physician was called, but only in time to see her breathe her last.

The sudden meeting with her brother was too much to bear þÿ excessive jov had Inirst the cord that sustained her bleeding heart; she opened her eves, giving evidnnee of n turning reason, they were east with alii etion on Henry as if she solicited his pardon; he tinderstood their meaning and imprinted on h r quivering lips the sad tok ui of affection ; one single smile like the flush of an evening sky, glimmered on her pale countenance, as if she would have said, / die content þÿ a moment more and her pallid eyes were closed in <1. aib. We saw her remains deposited in the due p mansion appointed lor us all, the dark V sib i-t grave. Henry erected a plain marble slab over the spot, and hastily quitted the eouno v that had seen the ruin of his proud anlivpa tions in the degradation and ioss of a in , ai loved sister. Years have passed since that period, and Henry has returned to the land of his nativity, a man of wealth, though his countenance still bears the traces of secret sorrow þÿ originating in the memory of the blasted hopes of early youth. t _ C.
